comparison_and_test: Inventory captures assets but needs an approved framework defining production scope, protection scheme, hardware/software types, lifecycles and inventory procedures; inspect all five framework elements.
Detection inventory needs asset-impact and contractual customer-notice links; trace an asset event to affected service functions and notice information.
Discovery reconciliation supports freshness; explicitly monitor the inventory-maintenance process and investigate stale updates.
Hardware/software inventory is a reuse candidate; reconcile its actual scope and fields to the approved AM-01 framework.
Reconciliation addresses completeness but must test accuracy, validity and consistency through lifecycle transitions and responsible-team updates.
Add asset-linked risk assessments and treatments throughout lifecycle; an owner/location field alone is insufficient.
Retain attributable history of inventory field changes; compare an update with its prior values and initiating event.
Entitlement review must expose users and rights for each resource; test the resource-to-user direction, not only user-to-group listings.
Verify hardware identifiers, lifecycle state and information needed for risk/security control per entry, including unowned or incomplete records.
Add software-to-consuming-asset relationships and risk/security metadata; reconcile deployed software against inventory.
Supplier support monitoring should retain communicated security-update end dates per software entry; distinguish unknown from supported indefinitely.

Policy lifecycle needs explicit asset-use rules for approvals, four data categories, configurations, software/support, installation, malware, remote disabling, transport, incidents, deletion and removable media; test each applicable item.
Local variants need framework-based applicability for the AM-05 lifecycle aspects; record why an aspect applies or does not.
Change risk review must precede production hardware commissioning and authorized approval; inspect a newly commissioned asset.
Baseline validation must test error handling, logging, encryption, authentication and authorization before commissioning approval.
Disposal workflow needs documented authorized decommissioning of provider-responsible production hardware, including the intermediate decommission event.
Verify permanent deletion or media destruction across customer, derived, provider and applicable production account data before release.
Extend authorized decommissioning evidence to development, test and staging as well as production when sharpened scope is selected.
Certificates need method-specific evidence that recovery is reasonably impossible; inspect residual media rather than accepting a disposal label.
Engagement acknowledgment must include asset-handling commitments before use for personnel exposed to risk-identified assets, including external staff.
Exit reconciliation must retain proof of every handed-over asset's return; missing-return tickets remain unresolved.
When assets cannot return by termination, remove associated access no later than termination; test remote assets and sessions.
Dataset classification must propagate to assets and possible labels across all four C5 data categories, including derived/provider/account data.
Intake/change review lacks an explicit annual minimum; add annual classification review and evidence of resulting updates.
Steward assignment is a candidate; require responsible asset parties to apply one documented protection schema consistently.
Sensitivity labels need confidentiality, integrity, availability and authenticity levels aligned with delivery/recovery objectives.
Architecture descriptions do not implement device-based connection authentication; test unique physical device identity in the connection decision.
Bind device authentication identifiers to asset classification/labels and test identity replacement or duplicated identifiers.
Detection routing must use asset protection needs to notify the appropriate stakeholder at the correct priority.
Test event ordering so higher-protection assets take precedence; generic severity assignment alone does not establish this rule.
Architecture review lacks a standby-hardware procedure; risk-assess and inspect protected storage/access for inactive production hardware.
Expand inactive-hardware protection to all hardware when sharpened scope is selected; test nonproduction storage.
Disposal custody does not cover all production-hardware transfers; add risk-based controls for offsite/alternate-location movements.
Require designated-person authorization before hardware transfer; inspect authority and timing against movement records.
Add physical protection, chain of custody and receipt verification for transfers; investigate a missing or tampered shipment.

Generic endpoint settings need the complete removable-media restrictions and narrow unavoidable-admin exceptions, encryption, malware scanning, disabled autorun, transport, sharing/deletion and third-party endpoint rules; test allowed and blocked paths.
Additional endpoint scope needs host firewalls, risk-based DLP, mobile geolocation and evaluated remote company-data deletion; test each capability separately.
A control registry is not an ISO27001-compliant ISMS; reconcile organizational units, locations, zones, regions and service lifecycle to management-system execution.
Management review needs a complete ISMS package: context, scope, SoA, service coverage, maintenance/improvement and last review results.
Commitment records must identify operational-control boundaries, exclusions and shared responsibility explicitly.
Audit programme is not certification; inspect valid ISO27001 or BSI-based certification and exact service scope for this sharpened criterion.
Validate accreditation/recognition of the certification body for existing valid ISO27001 certificates; a logo is insufficient.
Policy approval supports reuse only if the information-security policy is actually adopted by top management.
Add proof of policy communication to internal/external personnel and customers; workforce distribution alone omits customers.
Inspect policy content for customer security needs, objectives/level, commitment, strategy and ISMS organization, not merely version metadata.
Formalize the shared security responsibility model and its delivery interfaces/dependencies; a general commitment record needs this artifact.
Specify provider/customer handling of vulnerabilities, security incidents and other incidents at a level usable by each party's specialists.
Review SSRM accuracy across every offering under SP-02 cadence and changes; test an outdated offering.
Inheritance review must test actual operation/review of provider SSRM components; publishing the model does not implement it.
Notify affected organizations before responsibility/interface changes take effect with sufficient reaction time; retain delivery timing.
Conflict checks need risk-assessed segregation across IAM administration, development/release, risk management and operations where applicable.
Record and implement SoD mitigation in the treatment plan while prioritizing actual segregation; acceptance alone is insufficient.
Where segregation is infeasible, document constraints and operate compensating monitoring with timely response to misuse or unauthorized change.
Maintain a conflict/resolution inventory and enforce it on assignments, changes and revocations; one-time grant checks leave lifecycle gaps.
Monitor and enforce conflict-resolution measures, not merely recertify account existence.
Trace detected SoD deviations to timely corrective action and independent retest.
Advisory intake needs selected internal and external threat sources sufficient for the service threat landscape.
Correlate and analyze collected threat information for organizational impact; forwarding alerts alone is insufficient.
Trace threat intelligence into risk identification, assessment and treatment updates.
If German public-sector customers use the service, establish appropriate BSI situation-centre/CERT contacts; do not activate this condition without customer facts.
Risk methodology needs reproducible identification, likelihood/impact, acceptance/prioritization, owner treatment approvals, records and management evaluation including authenticity.
Quarterly risk reconciliation is a cadence candidate; verify the complete defined process runs at least annually and as needed.
Explicitly assess data protection differences, shared-resource separation, exposed interfaces, suppliers, cryptographic keys and tenant separation where applicable.
Test actual implementation of risk procedures relevant to delivery/operation; a completed generic register does not prove every procedure runs.
Retain delivery of risk results to relevant internal parties with scope-appropriate access.
Define purpose-specific risk information for relevant external parties and retain controlled communication evidence.
Quarterly exposure review must include annual owner adequacy review of analysis/treatment/approvals and focused review on significant change.
Add monitoring of risk evolution and corresponding reassessment alongside the annual/as-needed process for sharpened selection.
Evidence enterprise integration, leadership awareness/support and strategic alignment; a service-only risk list does not demonstrate ERM integration.
Include unusual/harmful internal actor detection in applicable risk scenarios, beyond financial fraud alone.
Use the assessed cybersecurity risk level to prioritize service treatments; test ordering and documented deviations.
Retain a documented treatment plan and execution evidence, not only assigned actions.
Verify treatment results reduce risk to a residual level accepted by its owner; approval before measurement does not prove reduction.
Provide full or suitably summarized treatment plans to relevant internal parties and retain delivery records.
Determine external treatment-plan recipients and detail from contract/legal requirements; record why disclosures are included or withheld.
Review treatment choices with risk owners every time assessment changes, using acceptance/prioritization criteria rather than waiting for the next quarter.
Map shared risks to complementary customer controls and explain them in user documentation; risk sharing cannot be implicit.
Extend change-risk review to all projects with direct/significant service effects, including nonsoftware projects, and evidence treatment where needed.
Add a uniform policy/procedure structure covering objectives, scope, qualified roles/deputies, outside dependencies, execution steps and obligations.
Verify availability and communication to relevant external as well as internal personnel, including accessible current versions.
Version control is a reuse candidate; inspect revision history and withdrawal of superseded procedures.
Verify policy approval by top management or a valid authorized body before effectiveness.
Annual/change review must use subject experts and consider organizational, technical and legal changes; a date rollover is not adequacy review.
Approve revisions before effectiveness and communicate them to internal/external personnel; test approval and distribution ordering.
Exception register needs explicit associated controls for every information-security policy/procedure exception.
Run exception risk analysis and owner approval/residual acceptance under the defined methodology; generic approval authority alone is insufficient.
Assess aggregate exposure from combined exceptions, not only individual accepted risks.
Set validity and review exceptions at least annually with risk owners or top management, including aggregate exposure.
Block exceptions causing deviation from applicable selected C5 criteria; retain source-permitted alternatives distinctly from generic waivers.
Check exception approval at the appropriate management level in addition to risk-owner acceptance.
Monitor upcoming expiry and review/approval freshness; react before an exception lapses.
Trace monitoring deviations to timely remediation; renewing an exception alone does not correct a deviation.
Exercises do not establish an ISO22301/BSI200-4 management system; reconcile the selected source and complete system processes before claiming coverage.
BIA alone omits BCM policy, leadership, interfaces, methodology, plans, resources, tests and improvement; reconcile all twelve documented programme elements.
Require a named top-management process owner and sufficient resources; generic delegated authority does not appoint that owner.
Inspect leadership actions encouraging personnel participation and supporting continuity effectiveness, beyond meeting attendance.
Expand site-loss BIA to development/operations, planned outages, degradation, time-dependent impacts and all applicable C5 data classes; test all ten source aspects.
Annual/change BIA review is a reuse candidate; verify organizational and environmental changes trigger review.
Exercise records need accessible, consistent plans covering ownership, activation, manual workarounds, customer communications, regions and incident interfaces.
Explicitly review continuity plans annually and after significant organizational/environmental changes; exercise scheduling is not plan review evidence.
Annual/change exercises need affected customers and relevant third-party involvement; supplier discussion alone does not demonstrate participation.
Trace documented test results into revised plans and future measures; preserve unresolved findings.
Add exercises using scenarios from past security incidents in addition to plan tests.
Provide timely customer notice of security-affecting continuity tests with time window and work description.
Provide potential security impacts and provider contact details for continuity tests, not only a maintenance date.
Review and adjust alarm/notification plans after each exercise; annual contact checks alone miss this trigger.
Obligation register is a reuse candidate only when legal, contractual and self-imposed requirements link to concrete compliance procedures.
Provide a controlled compliance-procedure overview on customer request; retain request and response evidence.
Define a multiyear audit programme with scope/frequency informed by change, policy and risk; an individual engagement plan is insufficient.
Audit rules need read-only access limits, safe windows, activity logging, configuration review, external penetration testing and internal security-code review.
Set and execute an explicit three-year audit programme for sharpened selection rather than an unspecified multiyear plan.
Record and enable contracted individual/group customer audit and information rights; supplier audit rights are not the same obligation.
Annual expert internal audits must assess applicable obligations, policy adherence and effectiveness of organizational/operational safeguards.
Verify auditors outside the reviewed line of authority or documented impartial alternatives where organizational size prevents separation.
Risk-assess audit vulnerabilities, deviations and nonconformities and track follow-up; severity assignment alone needs the defined risk method.
Document risk/feasibility decisions for automated monitoring of configuration, availability, incident response and recovery time.
Test automatic delivery of detected deviations to appropriate experts for immediate assessment/action.
Corporate reporting is not a real-time customer compliance interface; demonstrate the selected contractual checks through an actual customer interface.
Require regular top-management security information and at least annual ISMS management review of suitability, adequacy and effectiveness.
Operational metrics need business/security/obligation alignment and inclusion in ISMS review, not only weekly service dashboards.
Annual business-unit reporting must cover implemented risk changes, incidents/follow-up, control performance and planned security changes.
Verify risk-selected network attack detection and response safeguards are deployed and timely; architecture documents alone are insufficient.
Test layered defenses against irregular traffic, DDoS, spoofing, injection, DNS tunneling and IoT threats as applicable to the network.
Feed network-defense data to SIEM correlation and document/communicate safeguards; isolated appliance logs leave a gap.
Demonstrate prevention of unknown physical/virtual devices joining networks; discovery after admission does not meet prevention.
Specify zone/tenant separation, permitted protocols, distinct admin/monitoring traffic, office/WiFi/VPN and cross-partition/network rules.
Document risk-based trusted/untrusted security zones, including DMZ where applicable, and trace trust decisions.
Test physical and virtual network restrictions/monitoring against documented zone requirements.
Add annual and significant-change review of connection design and configuration against COS-02 requirements.
Risk-assess network deviations and track remedial measures through verified closure.
Periodically reassess business justification for every service, protocol and port, including compensating measures for insecure protocols.
Reconcile every network perimeter to an operating security gateway; inspect an overlooked virtual perimeter.
Cross-network authorization must use a security assessment informed by customer requirements, not only resource-owner approval.
Demonstrate redundancy/high availability of every perimeter gateway under failure for sharpened selection.
Separate infrastructure-admin/console networks from customer networks and enforce MFA; test a tenant-origin administration attempt.
Separately test workload creation, migration and orchestration networks against tenant reachability.
Where administration traffic lacks physical separation, verify current-technology encryption rather than assuming logical isolation suffices.
Implement documented tenant traffic separation at network level; application permissions alone do not demonstrate separation.
For IaaS/PaaS, verify physical separation or current encryption combined with logical separation/encapsulation.
Maintain current topology with subnets, zoning, outside connections and flows usable for operations and contractual recovery.
Indicate customer-data partitions, regions, zones or locations in topology/inventory documentation.
Reconcile topology to asset inventory and identify security, sensitive-function and customer/derived-data components.
Add at least annual topology review and timely correction of deviations, beyond change-time architecture review.
Transmission procedures must cover all four C5 data categories, listed interception/manipulation/malware risks and classification/cryptography links.
Inspect actual transmission safeguards and regular/significant-change review; approved flow documentation alone is insufficient.
Contract review must be supplemented by expert legal assessment of each government request covering customer, derived and account data.
Block disclosure/access until the assessment confirms a valid applicable basis requiring the request be granted.
Notify affected customers without undue delay unless the specific legal prohibition or clear illegal-use indication applies; retain exception rationale.
Constrain investigator access/disclosure to requested customer/derived data; test extraneous tenant data exclusion.
If clear separation is impossible, apply anonymization/pseudonymization so investigators can associate data only with targeted customers.
Monitor investigator activities as determined by the legal assessment; preserve attributable access records.
Remediate deviations detected in investigator monitoring promptly and retain response evidence.
Provide customers service-specific technical disclosure procedures, not merely a generic legal policy.
Documentation must explain disclosure process, capabilities/limits, logging, customer log access, methods and applicable notice laws for customer experts.
Version/review disclosure documentation and reconcile it with customer-data-access minimization rules.
Interface tests need standardized protocols/formats, authentication, untrusted-network encryption, integrity and backup/recovery plus current integration documentation.
Exit planning needs usable customer extraction tools or provider extraction services when size/format/architecture prevents self-extraction.
Demonstrate an application firewall protecting publicly reachable customer administration interfaces.
Internal IAM does not provide customer identity-provider federation; test the actual standardized external-IdP interface.
Provide integration documentation sufficient for customer specialists to configure their identity provider.
Contract exit clauses need format, delivery, availability windows, termination/access/deletion timing, customer duties and ownership/possession terms.
At least annually review legal/regulatory exit requirements and adjust agreements where necessary.
Include derived-data return in exit contracts and delivery when this additional criterion is selected.
Delete customer, derived and account data under exit terms; permit only the stated court-order or known future financial/legal exceptions.
Validate deletion against recovery using established forensic techniques; deletion command success alone is insufficient.
Provide customer-obtainable deletion proof scoped to its data and all relevant data categories.
Change intake needs recognized secure-lifecycle standards covering design, coding, deployment and operational vulnerability response; inspect implemented guidance.
Architecture must minimize provider access to customer data wherever possible; threat review alone does not demonstrate access-minimizing design.
Define and test enforcement of secure-development standards in the workflow, beyond distributing guidance.
For additional selection, prefer available CC EAL4-certified products or document risk assessment for choosing noncertified alternatives.
Outsourced-development contracts need equivalent security, acceptance against functional/nonfunctional requirements and verification against known vulnerabilities.
Pre-outsourcing assessment must address source custody/access, personnel practices, environment access and subcontractors.
Supervise outsourced development against the internal secure-development policy and equivalent achieved security level.
Provider personnel must run release-decision tests for outsourced changes; vendor test assertions alone are insufficient.
Reconcile change procedures to nine source aspects, including customer cooperation/notices, documentation, emergency equivalence, unexpected effects and increased security-feature testing.
Add regular role-based secure-development/tool and malicious-code training for internal and external engineering personnel.
Review the engineering training programme against changed policies, responsibilities and tools, retaining actual updates.
Security-feature design needs adequacy/effectiveness analysis and specified inputs, outputs and error conditions; generic requirements are insufficient.
Assess concurrent changes' interactions and cumulative service impact, then categorize/prioritize dependencies as well as each individual change.
Require high-risk change mitigation before production deployment; approval alone does not demonstrate mitigation.
Provide authorized customers preproduction risk-assessment information under contract and for highest-risk changes even absent contract, preserving the no-usage/security-effect exception.
Risk-selected tests are a reuse candidate if documented procedures cover development and deployment stages.
Verify test scope follows risk, testers are qualified or automation technically appropriate, and customers participate when contracted.
Before testing with customer data, obtain customer approval and anonymize while protecting confidentiality throughout; permission alone does not remove anonymization.
Trace every security-feature specification and error condition to tests documenting description, initial state, expected result and execution steps.
Use defined deployment-relevant severity criteria for test failures and initiate timely remediation/mitigation.
Add prelaunch penetration tests under the selected OPS-22 framework and record severity/treatment decisions.
Apply the role/right framework to source-control and deployment systems themselves; inspect privileged pipeline permissions.
Record every provider production change with attributable development/deployment/implementation actors, including out-of-band paths.
Monitor production changes against authorized roles and remediate deviations; release logging alone is insufficient enforcement.
Protect code confidentiality, integrity and authenticity throughout development; peer review alone does not secure the version-control service.
Track individual contributors and change dependencies and demonstrate restoration of affected components to a previous state.
Version internally/externally developed software, configuration and responsible commercial products; repository coverage must extend beyond internal code.
Rollback tests must preserve customer-data integrity and availability, including irreversible schema/data changes.
Retain deployed version/configuration history sufficient to reconstruct a past test environment under a risk-based, support-aligned retention policy.
Inspect authorized approval against defined test/approval criteria before customer production availability.
Include customers in release decisions as contracted and retain participation evidence.
Monitor the approval process and remediate missing/invalid approvals; individual approvals alone do not demonstrate monitoring.
Risk-assess development/test environments and implement protections including backups for necessary components.
Test production separation from development/test and block customer-data reuse without explicit approval; apply DEV-07.03's additional test-data conditions.
Prevent production-secret reuse in nonproduction unless unavoidable, with documented justification and source-compatible exception/risk handling.
Maintain current component lists for every developed/integrated component; top-level application inventory is insufficient SBOM coverage.
For unavailable integrated component information, document reasonable-effort infeasibility and treat the exception under SP-03.
Publish and maintain explicit third-party/open-source use procedures rather than relying on general change policy.
Record dependencies on hardware/software used in development, not only production runtime components.
Retrieve third-party software from trusted sources and verify authenticity whenever possible; retain verification or limitation evidence.
Risk-assess every procured development hardware/software product for this additional selection.
Exception/emergency change procedures must mitigate related risks and preserve the exception history.
Identify all production roles accessing each of four data categories or provider-responsible components, including non-obvious support roles.
Before employment, assess relevant internal/external personnel competence/integrity using risk-appropriate, locally lawful identity, experience, qualifications, record and coercion checks.
Role/status changes need risk identification and mitigation beyond merely notifying access owners.
Classify security-sensitive positions by risk, explicitly including administration and customer-data/production-component access.
Reassess competence/integrity before transfer or promotion into a higher-risk role.
Document screening intensity proportional to business context, information sensitivity and access risk, preserving local legal limits.
Define positions requiring recurring assessment and review their competence/integrity at least annually.
Validate employment terms against applicable legal/regulatory requirements before agreement.
Terms must bind internal/external personnel to conduct, security policy and subordinate procedures/instructions.
Confidentiality terms must cover obtained/generated information including anonymized and decontextualized information.
Deliver required policy/conduct instruction before access to relevant data/components, not just within a later onboarding window.
Retain documented acknowledgment of policy/conduct/instructions before access for internal and external personnel.
Target-group training assignment is a reuse candidate; reconcile all relevant groups to the programme.
Provide recurring and function-change training based on role risk and technical duties for external as well as internal personnel.
Update training for policies/threats and cover role-applicable component/data handling, incidents, practices and secure development.
Measure and evaluate learning outcomes; course completion alone is insufficient.
For sharpened selection, set at least annual role-based training plus function-change training.
Completion reconciliation is a reuse candidate; verify external personnel are included.
Trace overdue/missing training to timely remediation and escalation rather than only reminders.
Evaluate learning outcomes separately by target group, avoiding an aggregate pass rate masking a critical group.
Use quantitative and qualitative learning measures and retain assessment evidence.
Trace learning results into programme improvement and subsequent evaluation.
Disciplinary procedures require legal/regulatory review; investigation routing alone does not establish lawful discipline.
Verify violations and weigh nature, severity and impact under a defined disciplinary policy before action.
Inform internal/external personnel of possible disciplinary measures and retain delivery evidence.
Document actual disciplinary actions with appropriate confidentiality and authority.
Communicate surviving information-security duties and their duration on termination or employment change.
Base confidentiality agreements on identified protection needs for information and operational details.
Obtain service-organization confidentiality acceptance at contract agreement, not after access begins.
Obtain internal personnel confidentiality acceptance before access to all four data categories.
Review confidentiality requirements at least annually and on significant service change, updating agreements where needed.
Communicate changed confidentiality terms and obtain confirmation from personnel and service organizations.
If updated terms cannot be agreed, assess resulting information-security risk rather than assuming continued protection.
Remote-work rules need sensitive-data handling, access, secure networks/channels and approved equipment with unregulated personal devices prohibited.
Demonstrate actual technical and organizational measures enabling remote-work compliance, including an unauthorized-device attempt.
Key metadata alone omits a full crypto policy: protocols, hashes/salts, signatures, classification, lifecycle, rotation, law, change and agility; test all nine aspects.
Review against current BSI TR-02102 or suitable NIST guidance and record dated deviation analysis and risk-based remediation.
Add a documented PQC strategy; general architecture review does not establish quantum-threat treatment.
PQC strategy needs prioritized crypto inventory, current intelligence, hybrid methods and transition triggers/resources/success criteria.
Review PQC strategy, inventory and risks annually and on significant relevant change.
Crypto change assessment must include infrastructure, customer workloads, residual risk, cost/integration and customer notice of downstream effects.
Trace every crypto change to documented authorization, artifact and deployed state.
Provide recurring crypto-role training and change information, beyond generic security awareness.
Audit encryption/authentication/key practices at least annually and immediately after crypto-component incidents.
Review current technical suitability of cryptographic practices and implement needed updates.
Test current encryption/authentication for customer and derived data over public networks.
Verify cryptographic communication protection and personnel authentication for production remote access.
Expand transmission encryption/authentication to all data for sharpened selection.
Demonstrate actual customer-data encryption at rest, including relevant storage paths.
Test customer-only key access as the general rule and necessary provider access under IAM-07 with a specified exception procedure.
Agree key-use procedures and exceptions with customers; internal custody approval alone is insufficient.
Notify customers of key-procedure/safeguard changes that may affect data confidentiality.
Where a master key exists, regularly test related control design suitability and operating effectiveness.
Test encryption prevents recovery on resource reallocation or recovered media, not only normal read access.
Generation procedures must use secure randomness or keys derived from securely generated keys; inspect entropy/provenance design.
Maintain policy-aligned rotation schedules; communicate any risk-based nonrotation decision transparently to customers.
Certificate procedures need identity verification, secure issuance and trusted-CA acquisition; expiry monitoring alone is insufficient.
Verify identity and authorization before secure key provisioning/activation.
Record and enforce activation/deactivation dates for provisioned keys.
Separate KMS from application/middleware, restrict authorized access and enforce applicable geographic key residency.
Select a suitable software/hardware security module through documented risk assessment and test protected storage.
Archive keys under least privilege with recovery capability, need-based retention/destruction and complete storage/recovery logging.
Monitor, review and approve key state transitions including suspension and reactivation.
Restrict compromised keys to controlled decryption/signature verification; prevent new encryption/signing and preserve legal conditions.
Notify affected customers without undue delay of key compromise and cessation of encryption/signing use.
Expired keys cannot encrypt/sign; permit needed decrypt/verify, then destroy when unnecessary while retaining metadata and action logs.
If pre-shared keys or wildcard certificates exist, implement dedicated secure provisioning/use procedures.
Document HSM backup-versus-redundancy tradeoff, loss-of-control exposure and chosen measure effectiveness against obligations.
Exercise lost/corrupt key recovery, not merely data restore while keys remain available.
Monitor and document the entire key/material lifecycle with technical safeguards.
Retain creation-to-destruction/status history for non-ephemeral keys; preserve the explicit ephemeral distinction.
If external KMS is integrated, verify suitable certification, secure integration/access, rotation, monitoring and vulnerability/update practices.
For customer-managed keys, test secure BYOK integration, activity logs and authorized access; metadata custody alone does not implement BYOK.
Publish an RBAC framework and identity policy covering personnel and automated authorization components.
Reconcile policy to all sixteen aspects, including inactivity, emergencies, geography, compromise, approvals and privileged MFA.
Produce current effective cloud rights per identity; static role definitions are insufficient.
Review access logs at least monthly for unauthorized attempts and suspicious patterns.
Test personnel and automated identity grant/change procedures against the approved framework and policy.
Demonstrate technical restriction and verification of actual data/function permissions.
If break-glass accounts exist, define and test their secure use when primary authentication is unavailable.
Base identity management on risk and accessible data categories, including external personnel.
Define automatic inactivity/brute-force locking and withdrawal parameters with specific emergency-identity exceptions.
Monitor stolen/compromised privileged credentials and disable affected identities; login-failure alerts alone are insufficient.
Define controlled response when every identity needed to manage compromise may itself be compromised.
Expand stolen/compromised credential monitoring and disabling to all provider identities for sharpened selection.
Monitor authentication context and flag relevant suspicious events to authorized personnel.
Validate lock/withdrawal effectiveness, including active sessions and downstream components.
Remediate deviations found in identity-lock validation promptly.
Apply timely changes to human responsibilities and automated-component tasks, not only HR role changes.
Enforce privileged role-change removal/adjustment within 48 hours of effect; preserve the actual trigger timestamp.
Enforce other role-change removal/adjustment within 14 days; test late downstream entitlements.
Require the grant process again after revocation; do not silently reactivate old access.
Approve, time-limit and document temporary overlapping access during role transitions.
Review all relevant human/automated identities annually and on significant service change; nonprivileged cadence cannot exceed the minimum.
Use authorized reviewers knowledgeable about actual tasks, not arbitrary approvers.
Resolve review deviations by modification/withdrawal no later than seven days from detection.
Identity revocation must identify/reassign/delete production-associated resources and detect/remediate residual orphans.
Implement risk-based orphan prevention in nonproduction as well as production.
Quarterly privileged review is a cadence candidate; include significant-change reviews and demonstrate the six-month maximum.
Apply privileged-right policy to personnel and technical users for grants and changes.
Personalize and risk-time-limit privileged rights to necessary tasks; persistent broad grants need correction.
Require personalized authentication before use of anonymous technical identities.
Log privileged activity with enough detail to investigate suspected misuse.
Automatically monitor privileged logs for defined misuse events rather than relying solely on manual review.
Automatically notify responsible personnel for timely misuse assessment/action.
Apply defined disciplinary measures for proven privileged misuse, preserving lawful protected-reporting distinctions.
Include privileged container/image activity under OPS-10 logging, not only host administration.
Enforce MFA on provider administration interfaces and test alternate access paths.
Maintain current privileged-identity inventory and reconcile discovered grants.
Maintain responsible-person records for nonhuman identities and review six-monthly and on significant change.
Implement phishing-resistant privileged MFA with public-key/domain binding or comparable mechanisms; generic MFA is insufficient.
Demonstrate PAM enforcement of just-in-time elevation and just-enough access; manual approvals alone are not the required solution.
Partition service components from other provider systems and separate tenants; test both boundaries.
Test that compromise of customer-data components does not compromise access-management components.
Apply exact access-notice conditions for plaintext/no-prior-consent and contractual exclusions, preserving applicable legal prohibition.
Absent different contract terms, notices include cause, time, duration, geography, scope/type and retention of generated logs/copies.
Enforce contractual timing with a 72-hour maximum from access initiation; do not start this clock at later detection.
Disclose all possible plaintext customer-data access instances contractually before offering services.
Obtain prior authorized customer consent under exact plaintext/contract conditions, including specified encrypted-data and separate-key cases and derived data.
Consent requests need source-specified access details and an explicit customer response window unless otherwise contracted.
Pre-offer contractual disclosure extends to plaintext derived data for sharpened selection.
Contractually define cases where prior consent for possible plaintext customer-data access is infeasible.
Before direct/indirect customer-data access, verify appropriate assessment or supervision by assessed personnel, including support work.
Supervision must support real-time action approval/denial, end-of-use revocation, complete proposed/denied activity logs, person/device authentication and blocked data flow to supervisee device.
Separate customer administrator and end-user interfaces/access paths; role labels on one unrestricted path may be insufficient.
Authenticate personnel and automated authorization components across provider-responsible service systems.
Enforce production MFA for humans and automated processes; require qualified workload interpretation rather than silently exempting service accounts.
Production authentication mechanisms must meet the stated password/certificate/equivalent standard, with certificates governed by crypto policy.
Authentication policy needs risk/identity-based mechanisms and credential protection, issue, nonreuse, storage, renewal and strength with technical enforcement where possible.
Assess authentication obsolescence and implement replacement of outdated mechanisms or hosting components.
Every service authentication mechanism must disable an identity after a predefined unsuccessful-attempt count.
Require individual authentication before shared nonpersonal identity access.
Extend MFA to human/automated access in every environment for sharpened selection; retain workload interpretation as an explicit dependency.
Extend the specified authentication/certificate controls across environments for sharpened selection.
Issue credentials confidentially through an orderly process for personnel and automated components.
Credential protection must meet or exceed the protected component's classification.
Enforce initial-password change/self-creation, maximum 14-day initial validity, policy strength, change notice and current hash/encrypted-vault storage as technically possible.
Risk-assess credential-control deviations and implement resulting mitigations, not merely accept exposure.
Provide credential/password-manager guidance addressing phishing, social attacks and whaling to all responsible users.
Verify credential cryptography against the actual crypto policy.
Provider password-reset procedures expire within 24 hours and require subsequent user password change; customer PSS reset timing is separate.
Obtain signed confidentiality declarations for personal/shared authentication information with defined group boundaries.
Define at least sensitive and public physical areas covering all premises; network zones alone do not establish physical boundaries.
Document physical/environmental requirements from policy objectives, protection needs and risk assessment.
Facilities requirements need established technical rules and planning, drone/access, surveillance, lightning, fire, water, telecom, power and HVAC risks.
Utility maximum downtime must support contractual availability; service RTO alone does not specify utility tolerance.
For provider-operated data centres, specify expected CSOCs and how their design/operation are monitored.
Verify actual suitable CSOC implementation at data-centre suppliers, not merely possession of reports.
Define exceptional-event autonomy durations and maximum utility downtime under extended outages/heat/water conditions.
Demonstrate 72-hour external-power-loss autonomy or until all services transfer; preserve the alternative rather than imposing unconditional 72 hours.
Cooling design needs reasonably estimated lifetime peak outside temperatures with a justified safety margin.
Specify five consecutive days maintaining permissible cooling parameters at those temperatures plus margin.
If water-body cooling exists, determine sustainable durations at relevant water levels and temperatures.
The reference names two sites; verify actual service provision, requirements and adequate separation before claiming operational redundancy.
Demonstrate redundancy capacity and behavior meets the actual SLA, not just site count.
Annual redundancy tests are a reuse candidate; verify appropriate failure scenarios and effectiveness.
The two-site reference cannot demonstrate more-than-two-location survival of two simultaneous failures; keep a conditional architecture gap, not third-site authorization.
Selected georedundancy must meet SLA during the specified failures; an extra location alone is insufficient.
Inspect solid structural shell and physical protections against documented facility requirements.
Demonstrate detection and prevention of unauthorized physical access before service security is compromised.
Verify combined construction resistance of at least ten minutes from intruder detection; do not measure from a later alarm response.
Include surrounding walls and locks in the structural security assessment.
Where construction falls short, implement and verify compensating protection restoring the required security level.
Train data-centre personnel to respond effectively to unauthorized ingress and egress attempts.
Verify permanent presence of at least two guards plus video and burglary systems for additional selection.
Physical IAM needs two-month inactivity revocation with bounded exceptions, zone-specific factors/MFA, logs, post-emergency review and risk-timed visitor tracking/intervention.
Inspect entrance warnings stating nonpublic area boundaries and access conditions.
Demonstrate electronic site access authentication, authorization and entry/exit logging.
Verify structural, technical and organizational protection from fire, smoke, lightning and unwanted water.

Validate 90-minute fire protection or source-permitted equivalent/compensating routes with the specified 60-minute minimum where applicable; assess lightning, flooding and heavy-rain exceptions separately.
Inspect early fire detection/automatic voltage release, suitable monitored sections, suppression/oxygen reduction and fire-department alarm routing.
Add regular fire-protection inspections and exercises with corrective records.
Verify N+1 power/cooling, adequately sized UPS/EPS with annual tests, manufacturer maintenance and protected power/telecom lines.
Reconcile UPS/EPS implementation to SLA availability and actual load.
Qualified staff inspect lines at least every two years and suspected tampering, covering forced entry, documentation, wiring, unused conductors and unauthorized modifications.
Cooling must sustain five consecutive lifetime-estimated peak-temperature days plus margin; verify engineering calculations and tests.
Test telecom-network failure without loss of service security/performance through sufficient redundancy.
Align equipment installation/maintenance/servicing conditions with availability/security requirements.
Maintenance agreements must enable timely security updates of hosting equipment.
Monitor/control technical utility and building environmental parameters, not only software availability.
Automatically notify responsible departments when permitted ranges are exceeded and trace timely restoration.
Risk-based office rules need access, screens, unattended data, onsite document disposal, third-party-equipment prohibition and entrance alarms/cameras, with proportionate rented-office treatment.
Publish customer secure-use/configuration guidance and complementary customer controls; internal procedures are insufficient.
Reconcile guidance to all sixteen applicable aspects, including vulnerabilities, logs, IAM, crypto, tenant separation, distributed operation and interfaces.
Explain every necessary CUEC sufficiently for customer risk management; a list of acronyms is inadequate.
Bind guidance to the actual intended production version and maintain it through release changes.
Notify customers early enough to implement organizational/technical responses before planned changes take effect.
Test for vulnerabilities introduced during software development, beyond postdeployment scanning.
Risk-selected detection includes static/dynamic tests, expert review, SBOM checks and third-party-library advisories.
Assess vulnerability severity under defined criteria and initiate immediate elimination/mitigation measures.
Include annual code reviews or security penetration tests by qualified external parties.
Provide updated customer-facing known-exploited, patched/mitigated and no-fix vulnerability information, including justification and customer-operated assets.
Publish available and planned vulnerability remediation/mitigation details, not just an issue identifier.
Use component/SBOM data to identify customer-relevant vulnerabilities.
Customer advisories need CVE and current-at-assessment CVSS plus EPSS/SSVC or similar scoring with measure references.
Consult supplier vulnerability information at least daily, analyze service impact and risk-manage suppliers lacking daily information.
Customer-operated supplied assets need automatic update mechanisms with rollout after customer approval.
Disclose vulnerabilities using CSAF 2.0 or higher and the specified BSI TR-03191 requirements.
Demonstrate customer-facing error/log functions providing security status for customer-responsible components.
Derive customer logging scope from documented service-use risks before implementing detections.
Customer logs need actor/time/location access to customer/derived data, malfunctions and security-configuration changes where applicable.
Protect customer logs against unauthorized access/modification and enable customer deletion; internal retention alone does not provide this capability.
Where applicable, provide customer logging activation/deactivation, scope and verbosity controls.
Reconcile customer management-plane logging to all relevant systems/components.
Provide documented machine-processable customer SIEM retrieval interfaces.
Demonstrate MFA-capable customer authentication at every human/component/application access point; internal MFA is insufficient.
Enable customers to enforce MFA for their privileged users/components/applications.
Provide out-of-band authentication using separate factor channels when this additional criterion is selected.
Implement current, attack-resistant session management protecting all four security objectives.
Invalidate inactive sessions with configured detection; expose customer timing configuration where technically possible.
Customer passwords need first-use change/self-creation, 14-day initial maximum, enforced policy, change notice, 48-hour reset maximum and current salted hashes; provider reset remains 24 hours.
Supply customer credential rules/recommendations and tools to manage/enforce them.
Verify credential recipient identity and request legitimacy and protect distribution with additional safeguards such as MFA.
Provide customer-configurable role/right and access parameters; corporate grant approvals do not implement self-service IAM.
Test customer roles support least privilege, need-to-know and operational/control separation.
Provide customer access-review functionality, not only internal recertification reports.
If customer identities are managed, provide their currently granted rights list under contractual terms.
Enforce action authorization for customer users, components and applications; test denied operations.
Validate authorization before new functions and when existing authorization changes.
Route validation vulnerabilities into the defined vulnerability process and timely treatment.
Implement contextual multi-attribute access controls, beyond static role checks, for additional selection.
If SDN is offered, demonstrate procedures preserving customer-data confidentiality.
Validate new/changed SDN functions before release and risk-assess/correct defects.
For customer VMs/containers, provide image allowlists, version-change notices, provenance labels and industry-standard hardening.
Check image integrity/authenticity at startup and communicate results to customers.
Protect images/workloads against runtime tampering and communicate runtime status.
Technically constrain customer data and backups to contracted/selected regions; a flow diagram alone cannot enforce residency.
Verify suppliers also process/store customer data in customer-selected regions.
Specify customer, derived and account-data processing/storage regions and change circumstances in agreements.
Notify regional changes beforehand and obtain required authorization or allow contracted termination where prior general authorization is absent.
Extend technical regional confinement to derived data and its backups for sharpened selection.
Extend supplier-region verification to derived data for sharpened selection.
Selectable partitions must confine customer/provider identity verification and storage geographically; data residency alone is insufficient.
Confine provider/supplier privileged access, key handling and logging/monitoring within selected partitions, preserving narrow threat-intelligence and IP-routing exceptions.
Response procedures need classification, priority, escalation, root cause and incident/continuity interfaces with fast effective technical safeguards.
Establish an actual CSIRT with coordinated responsibilities; an incident commander label alone is insufficient.
Define customer channels and test timely appropriate notification to affected customers.
Add forensically supportable suspicious-system collection procedures, beyond generic report extracts.
Expert-approved response plans must cover identification through lessons learned and be communicated to relevant stakeholders.
Evaluate/update plans at least annually and as organizational/environmental changes require; contact testing alone is insufficient.
Qualified experts must classify, prioritize and analyze potential incidents, not only selected closed incident classes.
Document/share root causes and use results in evaluation and learning.
When external incident help is needed, select for competence/trustworthiness or national-authority recommendation.
Maintain an incident classification catalogue explicitly identifying customer-data impacts.
Correlate events using incident classification and assess correlated criticality.
Archive incident documents/evidence securely and tamper-proof according to criticality and regulatory requirements.
Reconstruct root causes and attack progression with traceability proportionate to impact/risk.
Simulate incident/attack identification, analysis and defense at least annually; continuity failover alone is insufficient.
Establish or contract a specifically qualified forensic/response team able to preserve evidence and custody.
Monitor incident-handling process compliance and remediate deviations promptly.
Send documented incident solutions to affected customers for contractual acknowledgment/confirmation.
Provide incident/confirmed-breach information to every affected customer and reconcile recipients.
Support customer active solution approval or defined-period automatic approval with traceable terms/events.
Contractually specify data available for the customer's own incident analysis.
Inform and where needed bind personnel/partners to timely reporting of known service-related security events to a designated central office.
Communicate that good-faith reports later found not to be incidents have no negative consequences.
Communicate incident reporting mechanisms to personnel, customers and service organizations.
Measure/monitor incident type and scope and report to supporting bodies; service uptime metrics alone are insufficient.
Maintain incident, solution and affected-asset knowledge linked to the classification catalogue.
Use monitoring/knowledge to identify recurring or potentially significant incidents and implement needed advanced safeguards.
Include actual root-cause results in evaluation and learning rather than treating RCA completion as the outcome.
Supplier policy needs risk/subservice classification, security/training/law, incident handling, contracts, monitoring and downstream application across development and operations.
Require regular independent design/effectiveness reports suitable for evaluating expected CSOCs.
When reports are unavailable, agree adequate information/audit rights for CSOC design and operation assessment.
Before service use, assess all four data classes/objectives, breach impacts, dependence/alternatives, CSOCs/deviations, diversification and downstream data processing.
Qualified personnel review supplier risk-assessment adequacy at least annually during use.
Deny supplier access to customer/derived/account data absent a documented exposure-risk assessment supporting the exception.
Obtain written customer authorization before service-organization processing, individually or through valid general preauthorization.
For sharpened supplier-access exceptions, add execution/supervision by authorized assessed personnel to the risk assessment.
Directory needs headquarters/jurisdiction, data locations, both contacts, service/risk class, start date and contractual compliance proof.
Review directory completeness, accuracy and validity at least annually.
Monitor actual security and legal/regulatory compliance against supplier procedures.
Review contracted quality, certification, incident/vulnerability, independent-control and downstream compliance information.
Tie monitoring cadence to assessed supplier class and inspect missed reviews.
For subservice organizations, perform procedures establishing design/operation of controls matching expected CSOCs; generic certificates are insufficient.
Analyze/evaluate/treat supplier deviations through the supplier risk process.
Notify all customers without undue delay of supplier changes significantly worsening provider security.
Review every relevant supplier's confidentiality requirements at least annually using a documented process.
Add automated supplier monitoring for configuration, performance/availability, incident response and recovery time.
Automatically report supplier violations/discrepancies for prompt responsible assessment/action.
Run periodic risk-scaled security assessments for every service organization and treat identified risks.
Document exit strategies for assessed very-high-dependence services, using actual complexity/uniqueness and source context.
Align exit with continuity and specify transition costs/impact/resources/timing, owners, success criteria and withdrawal indicators.
Document supplier flows/interfaces/protection and tell customers provider suppliers and downstream data types/customer-data processing relationships.
Annually verify supplier-transparency information completeness, accuracy and validity.
Sharpened transparency explicitly identifies service organizations and their subcontractors, not only their data types.
Prohibit direct supplier exchanges with functional components able to access customer data; generic egress controls need this rule.
Authorize incoming/outgoing supplier-component content before each transfer; onboarding approval is insufficient.
Automated authorization must trace proposed supplier operations, pretransfer verification and actual incoming/outgoing transfers.
Capacity procedures must include personnel as well as system resources; add staffing constraints to service forecasts.
Forecast demand/trends and manage overload; inspect a predicted exhaustion event and resulting action.
Plan continued contractual delivery during staffing/system shortages, including dedicated-resource promises.
Trace forecasts into SLA-aligned provisioning preparation, not only dashboard reporting.
Define monitoring, provisioning and deprovisioning safeguards and reconcile delivered resources to contracts/SLA.
Report capacity restrictions causing contract breaches through the incident customer-notice process.
Expose relevant customer-managed capacity/availability information through a self-service portal.
Where the service model allows, provide customer control/monitoring of allocated resources to avoid overcrowding.
Notify customers of significant actual/planned security changes in customer-allocated components.
Malware policy must cover system-specific measures, service components, personnel endpoints and all incoming flows.
Reconcile production components to required malware protection configuration.
Update available signature/behavior malware definitions at least daily and retain missed-update handling.
Generate regular protection-check reports and retain authorized review/analysis, not merely update success.
For the stated sharpened protection-program condition, use the highest applicable vendor-offered definition-update frequency.
Secure and monitor provider and customer management consoles against malware.
Automatically monitor malware-protection configuration for deviations.
Automatically notify experts of protection deviations for immediate assessment/action.
Backup/regular-restore policy needs applicable data classes, SLA/RTO/RPO, encryption, secure lifecycle, authorized restores, tests/customer requests and explicit provider-data exclusions.
Sharpened wording requires at least daily backup/replication and at least daily restore; preserve that wording and seek qualified interpretation before selecting an executable cadence.
Monitor backups across customer, derived and provider data under documented technical/organizational procedures.
Qualified staff investigate/correct backup incidents in time to meet scope, frequency and retention obligations.
Provide customer backup logs/results in a self-service portal; internal job monitoring is insufficient.
Set at least annual restore tests including provider data and customer/derived data where contracted.
Measure restores against contractual terms and actual RTO/RPO, including recovered-data usability.
Restore customer data only into environments with the same access restrictions as production.
Document restore tests and safe disposal of restored data, not only test success.
Notify responsible personnel/components of restore deviations for timely assessment and action.
Provide restore-test results on customer request with scoped disclosure controls.
Integrate restore testing into continuity management and its improvement process.
Transfer provider backups and contractually included customer/derived backups to an actual remote location.
Apply original-data protection needs to backups, including encryption and access restrictions.
Protect remote-network backup transfer through current encryption of data or transport.
Justify backup-site distance using recovery time and correlated disaster impact; two named cities alone are insufficient.
Verify remote backup-site physical/environmental protection equivalent to the primary site.
Logging policy needs events, enable/pause/stop rules, purposes/retention, authorities, customer transfer, timestamps and reliable consistent time sources with isolated-network context.
Restrict derived/account data to operations/security purposes, fixed purpose-related retention and protected logs; preserve precise anonymization/further-use exceptions and contractual delivery.
Contractually specify derived-data purposes except those inherent to general cloud operation.
Remove personal data automatically before log processing as technically possible while retaining utility for the collection purpose.
Include derived/log data in regulatory assessments rather than treating telemetry as exempt.
Technically enforce authorized log access, specified retention and purpose-based deletion.
Integrate relevant derived/provider logs into SIEM linking monitoring and incident handling.
SIEM must normalize/correlate, detect anomalies, alert in real time, report newly relevant facts and support automated response.
Validate event detection on assets selected through classification, not arbitrary demonstration hosts.
Remediate event-detection validation failures promptly.
Trigger incident handling without undue delay for identified events capable of leading to incidents.
Retain logs including SIEM in appropriate immutable aggregated form enabling authorized central evaluation.
Delete logs when collection purpose no longer requires retention, subject to resolved applicable obligations.
Authenticate logged assets and logging servers; use current encryption or dedicated out-of-band administration network for transfer.
Ensure unambiguous tenant-level user access identification across derived/provider logs.
Include traceable date/time in every event and validate clock accuracy.
Support forensic hardware-state and network-communication capture with a chain of evidence.
Deliver customer-related logs timely in an appropriate form on request for investigation.
Verify completeness/tamper resistance, clocks, identical evidence copies and source-system correct operation when records were captured.
Restrict logging/monitoring component access to authorized users with at least two authentication factors.
Route logging/monitoring configuration changes through controlled change procedures.
Monitor availability of logging and monitoring components themselves.
Automatically and timely report component failures to responsible departments for action.
Implement documented log/infrastructure confidentiality, integrity and availability resilience measures.
Test individual logging/monitoring component failure without restricting overall functionality.

Vulnerability policy needs proactive CWE-aware testing, CVSS/severity and EPSS/SSVC-informed timing, patching, nonremediation, incident links, traceable expert-support AI use and shareable configuration/advisory information.
Begin critical-vulnerability engagement timely including outside working hours; define what engagement entails.
Begin high-vulnerability engagement within one working day; this is not a universal one-day fix deadline.
Follow up regularly until remediation; first-response timing alone is insufficient.
Document source-permitted risk-based nonremediation and review assessment/compensating measures regularly and on significant change.
Add crash-specific classification/escalation/knowledge, access restrictions, sensitive-data protection, encryption, access-log review and retention/deletion.
Identify, record, classify, prioritize and address operational incidents under the defined process.
Identify/record/address component, partial-service and whole-service crashes, even before classifying them as security incidents.
Require qualified annual and significant-change penetration tests; vulnerability scans are not interchangeable.
Document risk-selected test types/counts and tester competence requirements in a penetration-test framework.
Identify provider-responsible relevant components through risk assessment for penetration-test scope.
Maintain plans covering all relevant components and specifying actual test targets.
For multiyear plans, test each relevant component at least once within three years.
Use CVSS version current at assessment for penetration-test findings and record the version.
Initiate remediation/mitigation under vulnerability-policy timeframes and track verified results.
Analyze penetration finding root causes for similar vulnerabilities elsewhere, not only the tested instance.
For sharpened selection, use verifiably qualified independent external testers at least six-monthly and on significant change.
Include prelaunch and postlaunch penetration tests under the documented risk-based framework.
Include applicable threat modelling in risk-based penetration targets for sharpened selection.
Base tests on architecture, configuration and source-code reviews.
Define a multiyear penetration-testing plan for additional selection.
Review penetration-test effectiveness annually and on significant change.
Use threat modelling of components, flows, boundaries and critical assets to prioritize highest-exposure penetration targets.
Correlate discovered exploit possibilities with past incidents to assess prior exploitation.
Measure/analyze vulnerability and incident procedures for continuing suitability, appropriateness and effectiveness.
Document responsible evaluation at least quarterly and verify resulting improvements' effectiveness.
Periodically inform affected customers of incident status and involve them where appropriate under contract.
Inform customers of actions taken when the provider considers an incident resolved.
Define contractual customer confirmation within a specified period that resolution addressed root cause.
Scan responsible service components at least monthly, comparing component data with current vulnerability databases.
Assess scan finding severity under defined criteria and retain rationale.
Initiate timely scan-finding treatment within defined timeframes.
Use scan results to update SIEM rules for detecting active exploitation of known vulnerabilities.
For sharpened selection, scan at least daily against current vulnerability databases.
Use CVSS version current at assessment for sharpened scan severity evaluation.
Define/monitor treatment-initiation timing under a risk classification including but not limited to CVSS.
Harden production service components to generally accepted industry standards and reconcile scope.
Document hardening requirements for each component, including unsupported technologies.
Validate immutable-image hardening when images are created, not only after deployment.
Retain configuration/log evidence for continuous availability of applicable immutable images.
Monitor deployed compliance with hardening specifications.
Timely report hardening deviations to appropriate departments for immediate assessment/action.
Use automatic hardening-compliance monitoring across provider-responsible components for sharpened selection.
Patch policy needs contract/vulnerability-based timing, maintenance windows, successful nonproduction tests and version-reversion mechanisms.
Align patching with the overall change process and preserve approval/test linkage.
Identify, test and deploy third-party patches through controlled change procedures.
Scan after patching to verify remediation and absence of newly deployed known/unmitigated vulnerabilities.
Automate third-party patch identification/testing/deployment with a defined manual-intervention exception process.
Demonstrate operating patch-deployment safeguards on responsible systems/applications, not only a policy.
Manage embedded third-party/open-source library updates with impact evaluation, timely patching and continuous verification against introduced vulnerabilities.
Document a cloud-layer model and risk-based customer/provider separation measures by CIA objective and preventive/detective/reactive type, including monitoring and deviation response.
Implement prevention, detection and response to dataset-separation threats under the documented model.
Test strict separation on shared physical/virtual resources against risk and cryptography policies.
Review separation risk annually and as needed, especially architecture changes, and adjust measures.
If confidential computing is offered, document purpose/risks, available technologies, protected stack/access limits, suppliers and TEE/enclave use.
Provide customers the specified confidential-computing capability/scope information in secure-use guidance.
Define confidential-computing responsibilities/law and technical confidentiality/integrity/authenticity safeguards preventing provider/unauthorized data or key access.
Implement TEE/enclave framework with interfaces, hardware/remote attestation, encryption/keys, monitoring, regular/event tests and trusted-base updates.
Where confidential computing exists, provide actual remote attestation for data-in-use protection.
Root attestation cryptography in trusted hardware/software and validate the trust chain.
Provide a customer interface to verify attestation integrity.
Define/document/communicate available attestation levels.
Include attestation-level information in customer secure-use guidance.
Container policy must cover image creation/testing, registry retrieval, deployment, operation and decommissioning.
Container procedures need inventory, risk-selected malware protection, lifecycle logs, separation, host IAM, feasible encryption, network detection, change control and hardening.
Add signed images/protected signing keys, runtime behavior restrictions and feasible recurring supply/image/dependency scans.
Verify actual container lifecycle safeguards implement OPS-34 procedures across deployment and retirement.
